a: Cold process soapmaking begins by carefully weighing all ingredients, then slowly adding lye (sodium hydroxide) to a liquid (usually distilled water) in a well-ventilated area while stirring until dissolved. The lye solution is allowed to cool while the solid oils and butters are melted and liquid oils are measured, then both are brought to similar temperatures (typically 90-110°F). The lye solution is poured into the oils and blended with a stick blender until trace is reached — the point where the batter thickens enough to leave a visible trail on the surface, at which point additives, colorants, and essential oils can be mixed in.

a: Trace is the stage in cold process soapmaking when the oils and lye solution have emulsified and the batter has thickened to the consistency of thin pudding, leaving a visible trail when drizzled across the surface. Light trace (thin trace) is ideal for intricate swirls and designs, while medium to thick trace is better for textured tops, embeds, or when working with accelerating fragrances. Over-tracing results in a batter so thick it becomes difficult to pour, potentially causing cracks, air pockets, or an uneven final bar.

a: Hot process soapmaking uses external heat (typically a slow cooker, oven, or double boiler) to accelerate saponification, cooking the soap batter until it reaches a 'mashed potato' or 'vaseline' stage where the chemical reaction completes in about 1-2 hours. Unlike cold process, hot process soap can be used within a few days of making since the saponification is complete during cooking, though it still benefits from a short cure for hardness. The finished bars have a more rustic, textured appearance compared to the smooth surfaces of cold process soap.

What is the difference between curing and saponification?
a: Curing is the drying and hardening period after soap is cut, during which excess water evaporates and the soap crystals reorganize to produce a harder, longer-lasting, and milder bar. Cold process soap typically requires 4-6 weeks of cure time on open, airy shelves, with weekly turning to ensure even drying, while hot process soap can be used after 1-2 weeks. During cure, the soap's pH drops from highly alkaline to a skin-safe level around 8-10, and the bar becomes significantly harder and produces a richer, creamier lather.

How does superfat affect soap?
a: A lye discount (or superfat) means using slightly less lye than needed to fully saponify all the oils, leaving some unreacted oils free in the finished soap for extra conditioning and skin-mildness. Typical superfat levels range from 5-8% for most bar soaps, while higher superfats (15-20%) are used for specialty soaps designed for very dry or sensitive skin but may produce a softer bar. Lye concentration (the ratio of lye to water) affects how fast the soap traces and how long it needs to cure, with a 33% lye solution being standard and higher concentrations (water discount) producing faster-tracing, harder bars.
